newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal bonds can close gap further on Bunds.
newsitem.headline: Portugal bonds can close gap further on Bunds.

text.p: The shrinking yield gap between Portuguese government 10-year bonds and Bunds, which fell below 150 basis points on Thursday for the first time, could narrow further as optimism over EMU gathers pace, analysts say.

Some analysts see the differential reaching 125 or 100 basis points by the end of the year even if others feel that such yields would be unsustainable because the Bank of Portugal is not prepared to see short-term rates fall too fast.
"We see a range of 100-125 basis points for Portugal against Germany by the end of the year," said analyst Mario Dias Vigario of Morgan Grenfell.
"This implies (10-year yields) for Portugal around 20 basis points below those of Spain," he added.

The spread between the February 2006 OT and the April 2006 Bund narrowed to 148 basis points on Thursday as Portugal was swept along on a wave of optimism that Spain will pass the test for entry to Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Portugal is better placed economically than its Iberian neighbour so if Spain qualifies, there will be no doubts about Portugal's entry into the single currency.

"There is a strong bet that Portugal will be in the first group forming EMU...even if it is all a bit premature, it would not surprise me that the spreads tightened even more," said one fixed-income trader at a large bank.

If Portugal were to enter EMU, this meant that by the second half of 1998, just a few months before the planned launch of the single currency, it would be logical for spreads between the OT and Bunds to be no more than 25 to 30 basis points, Dias Vigario said.

"If one believes that Portugal gets in, we are talking about a narrowing of the spread of some 100 basis points in a year and a half. These are the sort of calculations that have to be made," he added.
But other economists felt that the the long end was in danger of running ahead of the short end of the yield curve where the Bank of Portugal will be keeping movements under control.

"It seems excessive (a fall to 125-100 basis points). The rate trend at the short end will not approach the German level at the same pace," said Rui Martins dos Santos, chief economist at Banco Portugues de Investimento (BPI).
"I don't say it is impossible...but I don't see how it would be sustainable," he added.
He noted that short-term rates needed to stay at a reasonable premium over German ones or else there could be a sharp move out of escudos into marks.
"We could have exchange rate tension and that is a situation that the Bank of Portugal is not going to tolerate," he said.
The German repo rate is currently at three percent while that of the Bank of Portugal stands at 7.1 percent.
Most analysts see the Bank cutting the repo a further 25 to 50 basis points before the end of the year.
